In studying the play-off picture, it is possible that the National Championship could be decided at the Rose Bowl on New Years Day and not in the three CFB playoff games.

How could the system be rigged to decide the National Champion without that team playing in the CFB Playoff?

The CFB playoff could pick four teams that are neither from the Pac-12 or B1G.

The Rose Bowl has an existing contract with both the PAC-12 and the Big Ten (B1G) conferences. The conference champions or their secondary team would represent each conference at the Rose Bowl. In years where the Rose Bowl hosts the semi-final playoff game, then the two conferences can be replaced by the CFB selected opponents. However, in 2015, the Rose Bowl hosted the first CFB playoff game. In 2016, the Rose Bowl is slated to host the PAC-12 champion and the Big Ten champion.

For the sake of this argument, let's say that Ohio State or Michigan State win the Big Ten but are one loss teams. Let's also say that UCLA or USC win the PAC-12 and go one-loss in to the PAC-12 conference championship. If a two loss PAC-12 team is excluded from the four-team playoff, you could have other one-loss teams ranked higher than the Big Ten winner.

This could mean that a team like TCU, Baylor, or OU from the Big 12; a team like Alabama or Auburn from the SEC; and a team like Florida State or Boise State might be chosen ahead of a two loss PAC-12 winner or one loss B1G winner.

If the four team playoff has two teams with one loss reaching the finals and if the Rose Bowl pits a one loss PAC-12 team v. a one loss Big Ten team; you could have two national champions despite the Rose Bowl teams not playing in the CFB at all.
Could the 2015-2016 national championship be decided by the Rose Bowl and not the CFB Playoff?

In the situation where both are invited to the CFB playoff, then the traditional opponents in the Rose Bowl would be playing in the Cotton Bowl or the Sugar Bowl. Neither venue makes sense from an attendance stand point for the West Coast team to travel all the way to the South.
